---
name: check-sibling-candidates-first
description: In a refinement slot, read the sibling candidates' hypothesis.md in the same iter before building — the obvious graft is often already taken
metadata:
  type: feedback
---
iter_3/candidate_5 (2026-10-30): I built family_pooled_rule_prior + Beta-marginalised reliability. Its check passed but took 291 s per 200 draws (6 ms/grad, deep trees). Then I found that iter_3/candidate_3 had already submitted the same graft under the same name. I switched to family_pooled_win_stay_lose_sample (the WSLS model with the family-pooled hierarchical rule prior in place of the Dirichlet). That took 2.4 ms/grad and 115 s per 200 draws, with smoke loglik -835.0.
**Why:** sibling slots work in parallel and reach for the top-2 combination first.
**How to apply:** start by running `cat iter_N/candidate_*/hypothesis.md`. See [[wsls-exact-recursion]], [[number-game-refinement-findings]].
---
name: number-game-refinement-findings
description: Which refinements of the number-game Bayesian concept incumbent help or are dead ends (iter_2, 2026-10-30)
metadata:
  type: project
---
Tested in iter_2/candidate_4 (2026-10-30) against inferred_example_noise_concepts (MAP loglik -817.3, my per-row LOO -842.3..-842.9, p_loo ~22):
- Offset arithmetic progressions (c mod k) as an extra rule group: +0.4 MAP loglik only, so a near-duplicate.
- Bounded rules (rule ∩ interval): the share went to 0, so a duplicate.
- Family-only rule weights (7 families, equal within): MAP 16 nats worse.
- Hierarchical (partially pooled, non-centred) rule weights around family levels: LOO -841.8 (+0.6..1.2), p_loo 14, distinct predictions (RMSE 0.022). Submitted as family_pooled_rule_prior.
Data facts: 5 participants, each did the same 450-trial sequence (blocks of 450 rows), with no individual differences in yes-rate. Calibration by set size is already good and the residuals look like noise.
**Why:** the incumbent is near ceiling, so gains come from cutting effective parameters, not from new concepts.
**How to apply:** future refinements should target prior structure or parsimony; skip hypothesis-space additions. See [[interval-tempering-speed-trick]].
---
name: family-pooled-reliability-graft
description: Grafting family_pooled_rule_prior's hierarchical rule weights onto uncertain_reliability_noise_concepts — smoke OK but deep NUTS trees
metadata:
  type: project
---
iter_3/candidate_3 (2026-10-30): family_pooled_uncertain_reliability = incumbent (Beta-marginalised reliability) + non-centred family-pooled rule prior (softmax(family_level[f] + tau*rule_dev)). Check OK, smoke loglik -834.1 (incumbent smoke about -819 in-sample MAP; not comparable). Same 6 ms/grad as the incumbent, but the smoke fit took 290 s per 200 iters (~240 grads/iter: the tau funnel defeats the fixed Hessian mass matrix).
**Why:** the warm-start dense metric fits a Gaussian at the mode; a hierarchical scale near 0 makes the trees deep.
**How to apply:** if this is rejected as too slow, try a smaller tau prior or a fixed tau. Compare [[number-game-refinement-findings]] and [[warm-start-saddle-priors]].
---
name: complement-stray-refinement
description: Strays drawn from the concept's complement (not uniform 1-100) in the number-game incumbent — small MAP gain, distinct predictions; width prior is a near-dup
metadata:
  type: project
---
iter_3/candidate_4 (2026-10-30), refining uncertain_reliability_noise_concepts (MAP loglik -815.9):
- Interval prior ∝ width^gamma: gamma ≈ 0.07, -815.6, novelty-pool RMSE 0.0056 — a near-duplicate, so dropped.
- Strays drawn from the complement of the concept: p(X|h) = s^-k (100-s)^-(n-k) B(u+k,v+n-k)/B(u,v), with no j-sum. MAP -815.3 with the same parameters, pool RMSE 0.031, data RMSE 0.023. Submitted as complement_stray_reliability_concepts; check OK, 40 s smoke fit, smoke loglik -830.2.
- Candidate_3 in the same round did incumbent + family-pooled prior, so check sibling candidates' agent.jsonl to avoid duplicates.
- The residuals look like per-cell binomial noise (item unanimity PPC matched).
Scratch harness: iter_3/candidate_4/scratch/var.py + scr.py (VAR env switch; prints MAP ll and RMSE vs base).
**Why:** the incumbent is near ceiling; changing the noise model's shape is one of the few changes that still moves predictions.
**How to apply:** see [[interval-tempering-speed-trick]], [[number-game-refinement-findings]].

"""Refinement of win_stay_lose_sample_concepts: people learn the concept one
example at a time, holding a single working guess rather than the full
posterior. After the first example they pick a rule or magnitude interval from
the Bayesian posterior (the 45 Bigelow-Piantadosi rules and every interval of
1-100, size principle, 10% of examples drawn uniformly); as each later example
arrives they keep the current guess with probability `stay` if it still
contains that example, and otherwise re-pick from the posterior given all
examples so far. "Yes" is the probability that the final guess contains the
target, so the order of the examples matters.

The one change (grafted from family_pooled_rule_prior) is the prior over rules
from which guesses are picked: instead of an independent weight for every
rule, each rule's log prior weight is drawn around its family's level (parity,
primes, squares and cubes, powers, multiples, final digit, contained digit)
with an inferred spread tau (partial pooling, non-centred), so rules of the
same kind are similarly likely to be picked as the working guess.

The marginal distribution of the guess is tracked exactly. Write P_t for the
posterior after the first t examples, R_t for the probability of re-sampling at
step t and c_t(h) for "h contains example t". Then
  D_t(h) = stay * c_t(h) * D_{t-1}(h) + R_t * P_t(h),
  R_t = 1 - stay * sum_h c_t(h) D_{t-1}(h).
With the example-noise rate fixed, interval sums are precomputed in
prepare_observed. Sets shorter than four examples are padded with dummy steps
that every concept contains and at which nobody re-samples.
"""

import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt

NUMBERS = np.arange(1, 101)
MAX_N = 4
ALPHA = 0.9  # probability an example is drawn from the concept


def rule_concepts():
    rules = {
        "odd": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 2 == 1],
        "primes": [n for n in NUMBERS if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))],
        "squares": [n * n for n in range(1, 11)],
        "cubes": [n**3 for n in range(1, 5)],
        "powers of 2, not 32": [2, 4, 8, 16, 64],
        "powers of 2, or 37": [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64],
        "even": list(range(2, 101, 2)),
    }
    rules.update({f"multiples of {m}": list(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]})
    rules.update({f"powers of {m}": [m**k for k in range(1, 8) if m**k <= 100] for m in range(2, 11)})
    rules.update({f"ends in {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 10 == d] for d in range(10)})
    rules.update({f"contains digit {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if str(d) in str(n)] for d in range(10)})
    return rules

RULE_MEMBERSHIP = np.array([np.isin(NUMBERS, c) for c in RULES], dtype="float64")

INT_LO = np.array([m for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)])
INT_HI = np.array([n for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)])
INT_SIZE = (INT_HI - INT_LO + 1).astype("float64")

LOG_IN_RULE = np.log(ALPHA / RULE_SIZE + (1 - ALPHA) / 100)

FAMILIES = ["parity", "primes", "squares and cubes", "powers", "multiples", "ends in", "contains digit"]


def family_of(name):

    if name in ("squares", "cubes"):

    d_rule = p_rule[:, 0, :]
    gains = [pt.ones_like(q_int[:, 0])]  # gains[t'] = R_t' * prod_{u in t'+1..t} s_u
    for t in range(1, MAX_N):
        consistent = (d_rule * rule_c[:, t, :]).sum(axis=1)
        for tp in range(t):

        d_rule = s_step[:, t, None] * rule_c[:, t, :] * d_rule + r_t[:, None] * p_rule[:, t, :]
        gains = [g * s_step[:, t] for g in gains] + [r_t]

    gain_mat = pt.stack(gains, axis=1)  # (sets, t')

                  + (gain_mat[cell_set] * q_int[cell_set] * cell_frac).sum(axis=1))
    p_yes = pm.Deterministic("p_yes", pt.clip(in_concept, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)[row_cell])
    pm.Bernoulli("response", p=p_yes, observed=rating)


def _logsumexp(x):
    m = x.max()
    return m + np.log(np.exp(x - m).sum())


def prepare_observed(rows):
    sets = [tuple(int(x) for x in str(r["number_set"]).split(",")) for r in rows]
    unique = list(dict.fromkeys(sets))
    index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(unique)}
    S = len(unique)
    rule_k = np.zeros((S, MAX_N, N_RULES))
    pref_n = np.zeros((S, MAX_N))
    rule_c = np.ones((S, MAX_N, N_RULES))
    active = np.zeros((S, MAX_N))
    int_ev = np.zeros((S, MAX_N))
    frac_cons = np.ones((S, MAX_N, MAX_N))
    int_ll = {}  # (set, t') -> per-interval log likelihood
    later_in = {}  # (set, t') -> intervals containing every real example after t'
    for i, s in enumerate(unique):
        ex = np.array(s)
        n = len(ex)
        inside = (ex[None, :] >= INT_LO[:, None]) & (ex[None, :] <= INT_HI[:, None])  # (intervals, n)
        for t in range(MAX_N):
            m = min(t + 1, n)
            active[i, t] = 1.0 if t < n else 0.0
            pref_n[i, t] = m
            rule_k[i, t] = RULE_MEMBERSHIP[:, ex[:m] - 1].sum(axis=1)
            if t < n:
                rule_c[i, t] = RULE_MEMBERSHIP[:, ex[t] - 1]
            k = inside[:, :m].sum(axis=1)
            ll = k * LOG_IN_INT + (m - k) * LOG_NOISE
            int_ev[i, t] = _logsumexp(ll)
            w = np.exp(ll - int_ev[i, t])
            int_ll[i, t] = w
            for t2 in range(t + 1, MAX_N):
                cont = inside[:, t + 1:min(t2 + 1, n)].all(axis=1)
                frac_cons[i, t, t2] = w[cont].sum()
            later_in[i, t] = inside[:, t + 1:n].all(axis=1)
    keys = [(index[s], int(r["target"])) for s, r in zip(sets, rows)]
    cells = list(dict.fromkeys(keys))
    cell_index = {c: j for j, c in enumerate(cells)}
    cell_set = np.array([i for i, _ in cells], dtype="int64")
    cell_rule_member = np.stack([RULE_MEMBERSHIP[:, t - 1] for _, t in cells])
    cell_frac = np.zeros((len(cells), MAX_N))
    for j, (i, tg) in enumerate(cells):
        has_t = (INT_LO <= tg) & (tg <= INT_HI)
        for t in range(MAX_N):
            cell_frac[j, t] = int_ll[i, t][has_t & later_in[i, t]].sum()
    return {
        "rule_k": rule_k, "pref_n": pref_n, "rule_c": rule_c, "active": active,
        "int_ev": int_ev, "frac_cons": frac_cons, "cell_set": cell_set,
        "cell_rule_member": cell_rule_member, "cell_frac": cell_frac,
        "row_cell": np.array([cell_index[c] for c in keys], dtype="int64"),
        "rating": np.array([int(r["rating"]) for r in rows], dtype="int64"),
    }

rules as a group) and every interval of 1-100 (prior (1 - lambda_0) / 100^2
each), with the size principle and stray examples drawn uniformly from 1-100 --
but the learner does not know the reliability a (the chance an example comes
from the concept). It holds a Beta(mean alpha, concentration kappa) belief over
a and integrates it out for each example set, so strays are correlated within
a set. "Yes" is the posterior probability that the concept contains the target.

With n examples of which k fall in a concept of size s,
p(X | h) = sum_j C(k, j) s^-j 100^-(n-j) B(u + j, v + n - j) / B(u, v),
u = alpha kappa, v = (1 - alpha) kappa; this depends only on (n, k, s), so a

import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt

MAX_N = 4


def rule_concepts():
    rules = {
        "odd": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 2 == 1],
        "primes": [n for n in NUMBERS if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))],

    rules.update({f"ends in {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 10 == d] for d in range(10)})

    rule_k = pm.Data("rule_k", np.zeros((1, N_RULES), dtype="int64"))  # (sets, rules)

    cell_rule_member = pm.Data("cell_rule_member", np.zeros((1, N_RULES)))  # (cells, rules)

    rule_post = pt.exp(log_rules - log_norm[:, None])
    interval_post = pt.exp(log_intervals - log_norm)

    cell_int_share = (cell_count * set_lik[cell_set]).sum(axis=(1, 2)) / int_ev[cell_set]
    in_concept = (rule_post[cell_set] * cell_rule_member).sum(axis=1) + interval_post[cell_set] * cell_int_share
    p_yes = pm.Deterministic("p_yes", pt.clip(in_concept, 1e-9, 1 - 1e-9)[row_cell])

    unique = list(dict.fromkeys(sets))

        "rule_k": rule_k,
        "set_n_idx": set_n_idx,
        "interval_count": counts,
        "cell_count": cell_count,
        "cell_set": np.array([i for i, _ in cells], dtype="int64"),
        "cell_rule_member": np.stack([RULE_MEMBERSHIP[:, t - 1] for _, t in cells]),
        "row_cell": np.array([cell_index[c] for c in keys], dtype="int64"),
        "rating": np.array([int(r["rating"]) for r in rows], dtype="int64"),

"""Refinement of win_stay_lose_sample_concepts: people learn the concept one
example at a time, holding a single working guess (a rule or magnitude range).
They keep it with probability `stay` while it still contains each new example,
and otherwise re-pick from the Bayesian posterior given the examples so far.
"Yes" is the probability that the final guess contains the target.

The one change (taken from uncertain_reliability_noise_concepts) is the
posterior people re-pick from. They are unsure of the program's reliability a
(the chance an example comes from the concept), hold a Beta(mean alpha,
concentration kappa) belief over it, and integrate it out per prefix:
p(X | h) = sum_j C(k, j) s^-j 100^-(n-j) B(u + j, v + n - j) / B(u, v).
That depends only on (n, k, s), so prepare_observed counts intervals by (k, s)
for every quantity the guess recursion needs:
  D_t(h) = stay * c_t(h) * D_{t-1}(h) + R_t * P_t(h),
  R_t = 1 - stay * sum_h c_t(h) D_{t-1}(h).
Sets shorter than four examples are padded with dummy steps that every concept
contains and at which nobody re-samples.
"""

import math

import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt

NUMBERS = np.arange(1, 101)
MAX_N = 4


def rule_concepts():
    rules = {
        "odd": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 2 == 1],
        "primes": [n for n in NUMBERS if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))],
        "squares": [n * n for n in range(1, 11)],
        "cubes": [n**3 for n in range(1, 5)],
        "powers of 2, not 32": [2, 4, 8, 16, 64],
        "powers of 2, or 37": [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64],
        "even": list(range(2, 101, 2)),
    }
    rules.update({f"multiples of {m}": list(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]})
    rules.update({f"powers of {m}": [m**k for k in range(1, 8) if m**k <= 100] for m in range(2, 11)})
    rules.update({f"ends in {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 10 == d] for d in range(10)})
    rules.update({f"contains digit {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if str(d) in str(n)] for d in range(10)})
    return rules


_RULES = rule_concepts()
RULE_NAMES, RULES = list(_RULES), list(_RULES.values())
N_RULES = len(RULES)
RULE_MEMBERSHIP = np.array([np.isin(NUMBERS, c) for c in RULES], dtype="float64")
RULE_SIZE_IDX = RULE_MEMBERSHIP.sum(axis=1).astype("int64") - 1
INT_LO = np.array([m for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)])
INT_HI = np.array([n for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)])
INT_SIZE_IDX = INT_HI - INT_LO  # size - 1

END_0, CONTAINS_0 = RULE_NAMES.index("ends in 0"), RULE_NAMES.index("contains digit 0")
SET_CONCENTRATION = np.full(N_RULES - 1, 2.0)
SET_CONCENTRATION[END_0] = 4.0

# Constant parts of the (n, k, s, j) likelihood table; n = 1..4, k, j = 0..4.
_N = np.arange(1, MAX_N + 1, dtype="float64")[:, None, None, None]
_K = np.arange(MAX_N + 1, dtype="float64")[None, :, None, None]
_S = np.arange(1, 101, dtype="float64")[None, None, :, None]
_J = np.arange(MAX_N + 1, dtype="float64")[None, None, None, :]
_VALID = (_J <= _K) & (_K <= _N)
_LOG_BINOM = np.where(
    _VALID,
    np.vectorize(lambda k, j: math.lgamma(k + 1) - math.lgamma(j + 1) - math.lgamma(max(k - j, 0) + 1))(_K, _J),
    -1e4,
)
_CONST = _LOG_BINOM - _J * np.log(_S) - (_N - _J) * np.log(100.0)
_N_MINUS_J = np.maximum(_N - _J, 0.0)
_J_SHAPED = _J + 0.0 * _N_MINUS_J


def _betaln(a, b):
    return pt.gammaln(a) + pt.gammaln(b) - pt.gammaln(a + b)


with pm.Model() as model:
    rule_k = pm.Data("rule_k", np.zeros((1, MAX_N, N_RULES), dtype="int64"))  # in rule among prefix t
    pref_n_idx = pm.Data("pref_n_idx", np.zeros((1, MAX_N), dtype="int64"))  # prefix length - 1
    rule_c = pm.Data("rule_c", np.ones((1, MAX_N, N_RULES)))  # rule contains example t (1 if dummy)
    active = pm.Data("active", np.ones((1, MAX_N)))  # step t is a real example
    int_count = pm.Data("int_count", np.zeros((1, MAX_N, MAX_N + 1, 100)))  # [s, t, k, size]
    cons_count = pm.Data("cons_count", np.zeros((1, MAX_N, MAX_N, MAX_N + 1, 100)))  # [s, t', t, k, size]
    cell_set = pm.Data("cell_set", np.zeros(1, dtype="int64"))
    cell_rule_member = pm.Data("cell_rule_member", np.zeros((1, N_RULES)))
    cell_count = pm.Data("cell_count", np.zeros((1, MAX_N, MAX_N + 1, 100)))  # [c, t', k, size]
    row_cell = pm.Data("row_cell", np.zeros(1, dtype="int64"))
    rating = pm.Data("rating", np.zeros(1, dtype="int64"))

    lambda_0 = pm.Beta("lambda_0", 2, 2)
    set_weights = pm.Dirichlet("set_weights", a=SET_CONCENTRATION)
    zero_split = pm.Beta("zero_split", 2, 2)
    shared = set_weights[END_0]
    rule_weights = pm.Deterministic("rule_weights", pt.concatenate([
        set_weights[:END_0], (zero_split * shared)[None], set_weights[END_0 + 1:CONTAINS_0],
        ((1 - zero_split) * shared)[None], set_weights[CONTAINS_0:],
    ]))
    # Probability of keeping a guess that is still consistent with a new example.
    stay_logit = pm.Normal("stay_logit", mu=0.0, sigma=1.5)
    stay = pm.Deterministic("stay", pm.math.sigmoid(stay_logit))
    # Mean believed reliability and how certain people are of it.

Refinement of `win_stay_lose_sample_concepts`: people learn the concept one example at a time, holding a single working guess (a rule or magnitude range) that they keep with some probability while it still contains each new example and otherwise re-pick from the Bayesian posterior given the examples so far, so early examples shape generalisation more than later ones. The one change, taken from `uncertain_reliability_noise_concepts`, is the posterior people re-pick from: they are unsure how reliable the program is and average over that uncertainty, so strays are correlated within a set. One example that breaks a tight rule makes the remaining ones suspect too and pushes re-picked guesses toward broader concepts, while a fully consistent prefix strongly favours the tight rule. This predicts order effects (from the sticky guess) that interact with how consistent the early examples are.
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > $D/candidate.py
"""Refinement of win_stay_lose_sample_concepts: people learn the concept one
example at a time, holding a single working guess (a rule or magnitude range).
They keep it with probability `stay` while it still contains each new example,
and otherwise re-pick from the Bayesian posterior given the examples so far.
"Yes" is the probability that the final guess contains the target.

The one change (taken from uncertain_reliability_noise_concepts) is the
posterior people re-pick from. They are unsure of the program's reliability a
(the chance an example comes from the concept), hold a Beta(mean alpha,
concentration kappa) belief over it, and integrate it out per prefix:
p(X | h) = sum_j C(k, j) s^-j 100^-(n-j) B(u + j, v + n - j) / B(u, v).
That depends only on (n, k, s), so prepare_observed counts intervals by (k, s)
for every quantity the guess recursion needs:
  D_t(h) = stay * c_t(h) * D_{t-1}(h) + R_t * P_t(h),
  R_t = 1 - stay * sum_h c_t(h) D_{t-1}(h).
Sets shorter than four examples are padded with dummy steps that every concept
contains and at which nobody re-samples.
"""

import math

import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt

NUMBERS = np.arange(1, 101)
MAX_N = 4


def rule_concepts():
    rules = {
        "odd": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 2 == 1],
        "primes": [n for n in NUMBERS if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))],
        "squares": [n * n for n in range(1, 11)],
        "cubes": [n**3 for n in range(1, 5)],
        "powers of 2, not 32": [2, 4, 8, 16, 64],
        "powers of 2, or 37": [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64],
        "even": list(range(2, 101, 2)),
    }
    rules.update({f"multiples of {m}": list(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]})
    rules.update({f"powers of {m}": [m**k for k in range(1, 8) if m**k <= 100] for m in range(2, 11)})
    rules.update({f"ends in {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 10 == d] for d in range(10)})
    rules.update({f"contains digit {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if str(d) in str(n)] for d in range(10)})
    return rules


_RULES = rule_concepts()
RULE_NAMES, RULES = list(_RULES), list(_RULES.values())
N_RULES = len(RULES)
RULE_MEMBERSHIP = np.array([np.isin(NUMBERS, c) for c in RULES], dtype="float64")
RULE_SIZE_IDX = RULE_MEMBERSHIP.sum(axis=1).astype("int64") - 1
INT_LO = np.array([m for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)])
INT_HI = np.array([n for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)])
INT_SIZE_IDX = INT_HI - INT_LO  # size - 1

END_0, CONTAINS_0 = RULE_NAMES.index("ends in 0"), RULE_NAMES.index("contains digit 0")
SET_CONCENTRATION = np.full(N_RULES - 1, 2.0)
SET_CONCENTRATION[END_0] = 4.0

# Constant parts of the (n, k, s, j) likelihood table; n = 1..4, k, j = 0..4.
_N = np.arange(1, MAX_N + 1, dtype="float64")[:, None, None, None]
_K = np.arange(MAX_N + 1, dtype="float64")[None, :, None, None]
_S = np.arange(1, 101, dtype="float64")[None, None, :, None]
_J = np.arange(MAX_N + 1, dtype="float64")[None, None, None, :]
_VALID = (_J <= _K) & (_K <= _N)
_LOG_BINOM = np.where(
    _VALID,
    np.vectorize(lambda k, j: math.lgamma(k + 1) - math.lgamma(j + 1) - math.lgamma(max(k - j, 0) + 1))(_K, _J),
    -1e4,
)
_CONST = _LOG_BINOM - _J * np.log(_S) - (_N - _J) * np.log(100.0)
_N_MINUS_J = np.maximum(_N - _J, 0.0)
_J_SHAPED = _J + 0.0 * _N_MINUS_J


def _betaln(a, b):
    return pt.gammaln(a) + pt.gammaln(b) - pt.gammaln(a + b)


with pm.Model() as model:
    rule_k = pm.Data("rule_k", np.zeros((1, MAX_N, N_RULES), dtype="int64"))  # in rule among prefix t
    pref_n_idx = pm.Data("pref_n_idx", np.zeros((1, MAX_N), dtype="int64"))  # prefix length - 1
    rule_c = pm.Data("rule_c", np.ones((1, MAX_N, N_RULES)))  # rule contains example t (1 if dummy)
    active = pm.Data("active", np.ones((1, MAX_N)))  # step t is a real example

content.text:
I've written the candidate as `uncertain_reliability_win_stay_lose_sample`. It passes the admission check, which printed `OK`, with a finite smoke-fit log-likelihood of −831.4.

**What I refined:** `win_stay_lose_sample_concepts`. In that model people hold one working guess (a rule or a magnitude range). They keep it with some probability while it still contains each new example, and otherwise re-pick from the Bayesian posterior given the examples so far.

**The one change:** that posterior now comes from the incumbent `uncertain_reliability_noise_concepts`. People are unsure how often the program produces a stray example and average over that uncertainty, instead of assuming a fixed 10% stray rate. Within a set, one example that breaks a tight rule makes the others suspect too, so re-picked guesses drift toward broader concepts. The model therefore predicts order effects that depend on how consistent the early examples are. Nothing in the existing set models that.

**Checks:**
- **Equivalence:** I compared it with the original WSLS model with the stray belief made almost certain (concentration about e^8, mean reliability 0.9). The largest difference in predicted "yes" was 4e-4, and agreement was exact for single-example sets, as the approximation predicts.
  - Two earlier comparisons showed large differences. Both were test-harness problems, not model bugs: one evaluated the prediction in a way that silently draws random parameter values, and the other set the concentration so high (e^18) that the gamma-function arithmetic lost precision.
- **Speed:** the smoke check took about 10 minutes of wall time, though my test was running on the same single CPU. I haven't measured the speed of the full 30-minute-limit fit, and it is the main risk at admission.
- **Not checked here:** novelty against the live models and convergence (R-hat can't be computed from one chain).

The other refinement slots this round hadn't written any files when I started, so I couldn't rule out a duplicate idea. Slots 3 and 4 are refining the incumbent rather than the WSLS model. I also saved a memory note on how the count tables are laid out and on the precision pitfall.

Files are in `iter_4/candidate_5/`:
- hypothesis.md
- model_name.txt
- candidate.py
